guide.summary: Calendly OAuth is self-serve. Any Calendly user can create an OAuth app in Developer tools, and the docs describe no review step before it can access other users' data. The setup itself is easy, but a few details catch people out. PKCE with S256 is mandatory for every app, including server-side ones, which must also send the client secret. Each app takes exactly one redirect URI. The client ID, client secret and webhook signing key are shown only once. Plan for per-user rate limits, including a cap on OAuth token requests.

reasons_to_bring_own: Each app gets its own webhook signing key at creation. If you want to verify Calendly webhooks against a key you control, you need your own app.
Creating your own app needs no provider review, so switching from managed auth later costs little beyond a short setup.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth to start; you do not need your own app yet because Calendly has no review step, so you can create your own app in minutes whenever you need your own webhook signing key or control of the redirect URI.

prerequisites.text: A Calendly account to log in to Developer tools.
A redirect URI decided in advance. Production apps accept only https. Sandbox apps also accept http on localhost.
At least one scope chosen at creation.
Integration code that implements PKCE with S256.
A secure place to store the client ID, client secret and webhook signing key right away, because they are shown only once.

redirect_uri_rules: Exactly one redirect URI per app.
Production apps accept only https redirect URIs.
Sandbox apps accept https redirect URIs and http on localhost.

blockers.text: The client ID, client secret and webhook signing key are shown only once, and the client ID cannot be viewed again in Developer tools.
blockers.workaround: Copy all three into your secret store before closing the creation screen.

blockers.text: Only one redirect URI per app, so local and production callbacks cannot share an app.
blockers.workaround: Follow Calendly's advice: use a Sandbox app for development and create a second app for Production.

blockers.text: Only 8 OAuth tokens can be requested per user per minute.
blockers.workaround: Cache tokens per user and avoid re-running the token exchange in retry loops.

blockers.text: Deleting an OAuth app cannot be undone.
blockers.workaround: Edit the existing app instead, since its name, redirect URI, environment type and scopes can all be changed.

app_specific_gotchas.text: PKCE with S256 is mandatory even for server-side apps, which must also send the client secret via HTTP Basic auth during the code exchange. An authorization request with no code challenge fails.
The client ID cannot be viewed again in Developer tools after creation, along with the secret and webhook signing key.
Exactly one redirect URI per app.
Rate limits are per user and depend on that user's plan: 500 requests per minute on paid plans, but only 50 on the free plan. They apply to third-party integrations too.
On the Trial tier, Create Event Invitee is limited to 5 requests per user per day.

limits: No approval step is documented, so there is no separate unapproved state. Any Calendly user can create an app.
Sandbox apps are meant for development and testing. They allow http on localhost. Production apps require https.
Rate limits apply to integrations: 500 requests per user per minute on paid plans and 50 on the free plan.

unapproved_mode.breaks_at: No approval cliff is documented. The practical break points are: moving to real users needs a Production app with an https redirect URI; losing the one-time client secret or signing key means recreating credentials; and deleting an app cannot be undone.

steps.title: Get a Calendly account
steps.detail_md: You need a Calendly account to create an OAuth app. Log in or sign up yourself. The agent cannot do this for you.

steps.title: Decide on the Sandbox and Production split
steps.detail_md:
Each app has an environment type: **Sandbox** for development and testing, or **Production** for real users. Calendly recommends starting with a Sandbox app and creating a second app for Production. Do that.

Environment type can be changed after creation, so this choice can be undone. The agent can lay out the options. You make the call.

steps.title: Draft app name, redirect URI and scope list
steps.detail_md:
The agent prepares the form values:

- **Name**: letters, numbers, hyphens and spaces only.
- **Redirect URI**: exactly one per app. Sandbox accepts https, and also http on localhost. Production accepts https only. Use a localhost callback for Sandbox and your real https callback for Production.
- **Scopes**: you must select at least one. None of the provided claims names specific scopes, so check the scope list in Developer tools against the API calls your agent needs.

Name, redirect URI and scopes can all be edited later.

steps.title: Create the Sandbox app and save credentials immediately
steps.detail_md:
1. In Calendly Developer tools, open the **OAuth apps** tab.
2. Select **Create OAuth app**.
3. Enter the drafted values and choose **Sandbox**.
4. Before you leave the page, copy the client ID, client secret and webhook signing key into your secret store.

All three are shown only once. The client ID also cannot be viewed again in Developer tools. If you lose them, the claims do not describe a recovery path.

steps.title: Implement authorization code flow with PKCE S256
steps.detail_md:
The agent writes the OAuth code.

**Flow**

- Use the authorization code flow with PKCE. PKCE S256 is mandatory, and a request with no code challenge fails.

**Authorize endpoint**

- Take it from the discovery document at `https://calendly.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`. That document lists `https://calendly.com/oauth/authorize` and PKCE method S256.
- A probe of `auth.calendly.com/oauth/authorize` with a fake client ID redirected to the login page. That probe does not confirm the endpoint, so prefer the discovery value.

**Token exchange**

- POST to `https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/token`.
- Server-side apps must also send the client secret using HTTP Basic authentication.

steps.title: Add rate limit handling
steps.detail_md:
Rate limits apply to third-party integrations, not only direct API calls. Build backoff around these limits:

- **Paid plans**: 500 requests per user per minute.
- **Free plan**: 50 requests per user per minute.
- **OAuth tokens**: at most 8 token requests per user per minute, so do not refresh tokens in a loop.
- **Create Event Invitee on the Trial tier**: 5 requests per user per day.

steps.title: Test end to end against Sandbox
Create the Production app
steps.detail_md: Create a second app in Developer tools with environment type **Production**, an https redirect URI and the same scopes. Save its client ID, secret and webhook signing key at once, because they are shown only once. Then point your deployed integration at these credentials.

steps.title: Share with users (no review step documented)
steps.detail_md:
Any Calendly user can create an OAuth app. The documentation describes no review or approval step before the app can access other users' data, so there is no provider wait to plan for.

If Calendly does have a review process, it is not documented in the claims. Verify the setup with a second, real user account before a wide launch.

steps.title: Do not delete apps casually
steps.detail_md: Deleting an OAuth app cannot be undone. If you need a change, edit the app instead, since name, redirect URI, environment type and scopes are all editable. Only you should decide on a deletion.

drivers: mandatory PKCE S256 for every app

corrections.reason: conflicts with a better-supported claim: The authorize endpoint URL disagrees: c26 gives https://auth.calendly.com/oauth/authorize, while c38's discovery document gives https://calendly.com/oauth/authorize.

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, Calendly requires the app to be submitted for review before arbitrary users outside the developer's own account can connect via OAuth.
belief_diff.finding: The claims state any Calendly user can create an OAuth app from Developer tools and that the page describes no review or approval step before the app can access other users' data.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Calendly's app review typically takes about 2 to 4 weeks from submission to a decision.
belief_diff.finding: No claim addresses review timing; since the claims describe no review step at all, the wait time cannot be verified.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: Unapproved apps are limited to connecting the developer's own Calendly account and accounts they explicitly invite, capped at 5 connected users.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not describe any unapproved-app restriction or a 5-user cap; they only say no review step is described before access to other users' data.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Creating and using a Calendly OAuth app is free, but connecting users generally requires the connecting accounts to be on a paid Calendly plan such as Standard or higher.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say a Calendly account is required to create an app and give rate limits differing by paid versus free plan, but do not state that connecting users must be on a paid plan or that app creation is free.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: Submission requires a verified company domain, a publicly accessible privacy policy and terms of service, a demo video showing the integration, and a contact email, but no formal business incorporation verification.
belief_diff.finding: The claims list no domain, privacy policy, video, or contact email requirements; the only prerequisites stated are having a Calendly account and selecting at least one scope.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Redirect URIs must be registered exactly in advance, must use HTTPS, and cannot contain wildcards or unregistered query parameters.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm one redirect URI per app and that Production allows only https while Sandbox also allows http on localhost; they say nothing about exact pre-registration, wildcards, or query parameters.
